title: A Number in English Words

concept.title: A big number is a smaller number, a name and a rest
body: English reads a number by splitting it into pieces: `1234567` is "one million" + "two hundred thirty four thousand" + "five hundred sixty seven". Each piece before a name (`thousand`, `million`, `billion`) is itself a number below 1000, so it is read by the **same function**. And "two hundred thirty four" is "two hundred" followed by the number `34`, again read by the same function.

The ranges are checked from the smallest to the biggest, and a part that is zero is skipped (1000 is just "one thousand"). Splitting a problem into "a smaller number, a name, and the rest" and reusing the function for both numbers is a typical use of recursion.

statement: Write the integer `n` in English words in lowercase, using single spaces and no hyphens and no word `and`. Use `zero`, `one` ... `nineteen`, then `twenty`, `thirty`, ..., `ninety` (a number such as 21 is `twenty one`), `hundred`, `thousand`, `million` and `billion`. A part that is zero is not written (1000 is `one thousand`).
outputFormat: Print the words on one line.

examples.output: one thousand two hundred thirty four
examples.note: one thousand, two hundred, thirty, four: "one thousand two hundred thirty four".

hints: Numbers below 20 are single words from a table; tens (20 to 90) are single words too.
For a number below 1000, say the hundreds digit and the word hundred, then say the rest with the same function.
For a bigger number split off the largest of billion, million, thousand and say the two parts with the same function.

explanation: Numbers below 20 and the tens come from tables. A number below 1000 is its hundreds word plus the rest; a bigger number is split by the largest of billion, million and thousand into a smaller number, the name, and the rest, and the same function reads both numbers.
solution.complexity: Time O(1) for these sizes (a handful of calls).
